questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Where is the signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein located?
options: Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Inside the membrane at the C-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the C-terminal end
questions.correct_answer: Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end
questions.explanation:
The signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein is located inside the membrane (transmembrane region).

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane). 

Integral membrane proteins or transmembrane proteins are embedded in the cell membrane, spanning through the entire thickness. They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions and require the use of detergent for solubility.  Examples are ligand-binding receptors for hormones or neurotransmitters, transport proteins like Na+-K+ ATPase, pores, ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and GTP-binding proteins (G proteins). 

Peripheral proteins are attached only to one surface of the cell membrane and do not penetrate all the way through. They are often attached to integral proteins. Examples are cell surface receptors, enzymes, ankyrin.



Signaling sequences are 16 to 30 amino acid residues in length and located at the N-terminal extension of the membrane proteins. After an appropriate trigger, they are either cleaved (and bind to MHC class I of the endoplasmic reticulum) or act as a membrane anchor (transporting proteins across the membrane).

Integral proteins can be divided into:

  • Type I integral proteins have a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence (towards the cytosol). Examples include histocompatibility antigens, glycophorin, and membrane immunoglobulin.
  • Type II integral proteins have a non-cleavable N terminal combined signal/anchor sequence. Examples include transferrin receptors and glycosyl transferases.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Which of the following primary second messengers is involved in the contraction of ciliary muscles while focusing on near objects?
questions.explanation:
IP3 is the primary second messenger involved in the contraction of ciliary muscles to focus on a near object.

On focusing on a near object, stimulation of the parasympathetic nerve fibers leads to the contraction of the bilateral ciliary muscle, via short ciliary nerves, which relaxes the lens ligaments. The lens becomes thicker and the increase in the refractive index allows the eye to focus on the near object. This is known as the accommodation reflex.

In the ciliary muscles of the eye, contraction is mediated via M3 > M2 receptors, while relaxation is mediated via the β2 receptor.

M3 receptors act via the formation of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), leading to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ and activation of protein kinase C, respectively. The increase in intracellular Ca2+ sets up a chain reaction which eventually leads to contraction of the ciliary smooth muscle of the eye.

Thus, in the contraction of the ciliary muscle during focusing on a near object, the second messenger involved is the IP3-DAG pathway.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: The second phase of saliva secretion involves:
options: Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, passive K+ secretion, active secretion of HCO3-
Passive Na+ reabsorption, active Cl- reabsorption, passive K+ secretion, active secretion of HCO3-
Passive Na+ secretion, active Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-
Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-
questions.correct_answer: Active Na+ reabsorption, passive Cl- reabsorption, active K+ secretion, passive secretion of HCO3-
questions.explanation:
During the second phase of salivary secretion, Na+ is actively reabsorbed, Cl-  is reabsorbed passively, K+ is secreted actively and HCO3- is secreted passively (part of the secretion may be active as well, but among the given options, option D is the most accurate with respect to all the ions).

Salivary secretion occurs in two stages:

The first stage involves acini, which secrete ptyalin and/or mucin together with some ions. The composition of the ions is similar to that of the extra-cellular fluid.

The second stage involves the ducts. As the primary salivary secretion flows through the ducts, two active transport processes occur:

  • Na+ is actively re-absorbed and K+ is actively secreted, in exchange for Na+.
  • HCO3- is secreted by the ductal epithelium into the lumen of the salivary ducts. Some of this secretion occurs by passive bicarbonate exchange for Cl- and partly active secretion.

As a result, the Na+ and Cl- concentrations are lower than that of plasma, while K+ and HCO3- concentrations are higher than that of plasma.

Macula forms the part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.



 

Signals from the renal tubules affect filtration in its glomerulus. As the rate of flow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases, and vice versa. This is known as tubuloglomerular feedback which maintains the constancy of the load delivered to the distal tubule.

The sensor is the macula densa. The Na+ and Cl− in the fluid enter the macula densa cells via theNa+–K–2Cl− cotransporter in their apical membranes. The increased Na+ increases the Na+-K+ ATPase activity causing ATP hydrolysis and the formation of adenosine. questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question:
Which of the following can be used to calculate the cardiac output?

A. ECHO.
B. Ventilation-perfusion scan.
C. Thermodilution.
D. Fick's principle
questions.explanation:
Fick principle, thermodilution, and ECHO can be used to measure cardiac output.

Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart into the aorta every minute. The average cardiac output is 5L/min and can be measured by various indirect methods.

Fick's principle uses the total amount of oxygen absorbed from the air by the lungs and the arteriovenous oxygen difference of blood to calculate the cardiac output using the following formula:

Cardiac output (L/min) = (O2 absorbed per minute by the lungs (mL/min))  /  (Arterio-venous O2 difference(mL/L of blood))                                       

Thermodilution method employs cold saline which is infused into the right atrium through a double-lumen Swan–Ganz thermodilution catheter and the temperature change is measured at the pulmonary artery using a thermistor at the end of the catheter. The mean decrease in the temperature of blood is inversely proportional to the cardiac output.

An ECHO uses ultrasound waves from a transducer placed on the chest wall to measure the velocity of blood flowing from the left ventricle into the aorta. Stroke volume can be calculated from this. Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.

The other methods that can be used to measure cardiac output include impedance cardiography a.k.a. thoracic electrical bioimpedance, electromagnetic or ultrasonic flowmeter,and  indicator dilution method.

Ventilation-perfusion scan is not a method of cardiac output measurement. It is used to assess pulmonary circulation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question:
A woman has vomiting whenever she eats spicy food. Arrange the sequence of events during vomiting.
  1. LES is open and UES is closed.
  2. Strong contractions in the stomach.
  3. Inspiration against a closed glottis. 
  4. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter. 
  5. LES opens and UES opens.
  6. Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine.

LES: Lower esophageal sphincter 

UES: Upper esophageal sphincter
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence of vomiting is 6, 4, 2, 3, 1, 5.

6. Reverse peristalsis in the small intestine.
4. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter. 
2. Strong contractions in the stomach.
3. Inspiration against a closed glottis. 
1. LES is open and UES is closed.
5. LES opens and UES opens.

The sensory signals that initiate vomiting are located in the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and upper portions of the small intestines. Excessive distention or irritation of the duodenum provides a strong stimulus for vomiting. Area postrema constitutes the vomiting centre.

In the early stage, reverse peristalsis begins often minutes before vomiting. It begins far down in the ileum and travels up the intestine. This process pushes a large share of lower small intestine contents to the duodenum and stomach. Relaxation of the pyloric sphincter occurs during this process.

At the onset of vomiting, strong intrinsic contractions are seen in the duodenum and stomach. Once the vomiting centre has been stimulated, inspiration occurs against the closed glottis. It prevents the flow of vomitus into the lungs. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is open and the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) is closed at this stage.

The muscles of the abdominal wall contract, building intra-gastric pressure. Finally LES relaxes completely and UES also relaxes allowing the expulsion of the gastric contents.

Note: The esophageal smooth muscle functions as LES at the gastro-esophageal junction. It normally remains tonically constricted. Receptive relaxation of LES occurs when the peristaltic wave passes down the esophagus.

Convergence means signals from multiple inputs uniting to excite a single neuron. It can be of 2 types:

questions.question: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity could be seen in blood volume control by the kidney.

When the blood volume falls below the equilibrium, the renal–body fluid mechanism causes the blood volume returns back to the equilibrium point resulting in zero error and hence the gain of kidney in its ability to regulate blood volume is infinity (∞).

The degree of effectiveness with which a regulatory system maintains constant conditions is determined by the gain of the negative feedback system. 

Gain= Correction/Error

Example: If an external or internal factor led to a decrease in mean blood pressure from 100 mm Hg to 80 mm Hg. Activation of a negative feedback mechanism i.e. baroreflex leads to a correction of blood pressure to 96 mm Hg. So in this case,

  • Correction = 16 mm Hg
  • Error = 4 mm Hg
  • Gain = Correction/Error = 16/4 = 4

Note: A gain of 0 would imply a total failure of the regulatory system and a gain of infinity (∞) would indicate complete restoration of the regulated variable.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
questions.explanation:
The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period. It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction.

In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second.
Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds.

In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves.
Hence, the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds.

Substituting the value in the formula, we get:
Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100/5 = 20/sec.



Tetanization:

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

  • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
  • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

  • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
  • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Least frequency of slow waves is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER) also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65mV and -45mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:

  • Stomach: 4/min
  • Duodenum: 12/min
  • Distal ileum: 8/min
  • Cecum: 2/min
  • Sigmoid colon: 6/min

The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.



Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Macula densa is formed by which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation:
Macula densa is formed by specialized tubular epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule.



The juxtaglomerular apparatus consists of the following parts:

  • Macula densa: At the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle, and at the beginning of the distal tubule, the tubular epithelial cells are specialized to form the macula densa. They detect sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate. This happens as follows: When there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.
  • Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.
  • Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: This is the graph depicting the filterability of dextran through the kidney, 1 representing complete filtration and 0 representing no filtration. Choose the substance A, B, C respectively.
questions.explanation:
In the given graph, the order of filterability is A>B>C, which likely indicates that the substances are Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic.

The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most of the negative charged (anionic substances). Whereas, the cationic substances are easily filtered.

Hence, the order of filterability would be: Polycationic > Neutral > Polyanionic, represented by A, B, and C in the graph shown.

The glomerular filtration barrier consists of:

  • Endothelium of the capillary
  • Basement membrane: 
    • Lamina densa - electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen
    • Lamina rara interna - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge
    • Lamina rara externa - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge
  • Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane

The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, which measure from 4 nm up to 8nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of less than 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approaches zero.

However, in addition to the size of the particles, the filtration also depends mainly on the charge of the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively charged proteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). The property can be studied by using charged dextran.

When the filtration of the negatively and positively charged dextrans was studied, the results indicated that the negatively charged dextrans in the blood are repelled, with the result that filtration of anionic substances 4 nm in diameter is less than half that of neutral substances of the same size.

This explains, why albumin despite having an effective molecular diameter of approximately 7 nm, has a very low filtration rate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question:
Which of the following statements is true about skeletal muscle contraction?
  1. Extracellular Ca2+ is not important for contraction
  2. Ca2+ is released from mitochondria
  3. Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  4. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on sarcolemma have no role in EC coupling
questions.explanation:
During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Only statement 3 is correct.

Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:

  • Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
  • This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
  • When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an action potential is generated.
  • The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread of depolarisation.
  • The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.
  • The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
  • The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.

Steps in relaxation:

  • The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action of SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase).
  • Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, and the muscle relaxes. 
 
Other options:
 
Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction. When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodium channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodium concentration causes sustained depolarization, which may lead to tetany.
 
Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
 
Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sarcolemma) are activated by a depolarizing stimulus, which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increased calcium concentration will eventually lead to muscle contraction.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding mechanisms of depolarisation, repolarisation, and hyperpolarisation in a skeletal muscle action potential?
  1. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through voltage-gated channels
  2. Depolarisation due to influx of Na+ through ligand-gated channels
  3. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a voltage-gated channel
  4. Repolarisation due to efflux of K+ through a ligand-gated channel
  5. Hyperpolarisation due to efflux of K+
questions.explanation:
Statements 1, 3, and 5 are correct.

Action potential in skeletal muscle:

  • Motor-neuron discharge causes end-plate potential, which when reaches to a threshold value, causes action potential in the muscle fibre.
  • The depolarization of the muscle fibre is caused by the activation of the voltage-gated sodium channels, which causes the influx of sodium.
  • During repolarization, the sodium channels are closed, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, which causes efflux of potassium.
  • The voltage-gated potassium channels close slowly. As a result, the potassium efflux continues, leading to hyperpolarization of the membrane.


The steps in an action potential in muscle fibre and the neuron, are similar except for the quantitative differences, such as:

  • RMP is -80 to -90 mV in skeletal muscle fibres, while it is about -70mV in neurons.
  • The duration of the action potential in skeletal muscle is 1 to 5 msec, which is about 5 times longer than in the largest myelinated nerve fibre.
  • The velocity of conduction is about 3-5m/s, which is about 1/13th of the velocity of the nerve fibre.

  • The T wave of ECG occurs during ventricular repolarization, which is followed by the opening of the mitral valve, followed by rapid filling phase of the ventricle (second  phase of ventricular diastole).

  2. TLC

In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal. Hence, both 1 and 2 are correct.

The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs.

  • The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level.

  • The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________
options: Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
questions.explanation:
Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing.

  • These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla.
  • These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration.
  • These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons.

Breathing is under the control of both the following:

  • Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract)
  • Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle).

There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.

 

Inspiration
Initiation Pre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla
Maintenance Apneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
Termination  Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center


Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise.

Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

questions.question: 7. During a simple muscle twitch experiment, latent period = 10 ms, contraction period = 40 ms, relaxation period= 20 ms. What is the fusion frequency that is required to tetanize this muscle in Hz.
questions.explanation:
The tetanising frequency of the given skeletal muscle is 25 per second. Tetanising frequency = 1/contraction period (per second) Therefore, tetanising frequency = 1/40 per millisecond = 1000/40 per second = 25 per second = 25 Hz With repeated stimulation, contraction occurs repeatedly before any relaxation has occurred. This causes the individual responses to fuse into one continuous contraction. Such a response is called tetanus (tetanic contraction). ​​​Tetanising frequency is the minimum frequency required for producing tetanus. Tetanus is of two types: complete tetanus, when no relaxation occurs between stimuli, and incomplete tetanus, when periods of incomplete relaxation occur between the summated stimuli.  When there is a repeated stimulus to a muscle fibre before relaxation, it produces an additional contraction of the muscle. The second contraction adds to the first contraction and the total strength of contraction increases. This phenomenon is known as a summation of contractions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: 8. Which of the following is an example of a feedforward mechanism in homeostasis?
options: Increased cardiac output in severe anemia
Increase heart rate when standing up from supine position
questions.explanation:
Vasoconstriction on cooling of the skin is an example of a feedforward mechanism in homeostasis. Feed-forward control is used to apprise the brain whether a muscle movement is performed correctly. If not, the brain corrects the feed-forward signals that it sends to the muscle the next time the movement is required. This mechanism is often called adaptive control. Examples include * Temperature regulation – The hypothalamus initiates thermoregulatory responses before the changes in environmental temperature have succeeded in changing the body’s core body temperature * Stimulation of gastric acid secretion * Parathyroid hormone stimulating the production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D Other options: Options A, B and D: Increased cardiac output in severe anaemia, increased vasopressin secretion during dehydration and increased heart rate when standing up from the supine position are all examples of negative feedback mechanism.

questions.question: 9. During the recording of the EEG, a resting and awake person was instructed to close his eyes and then open them. The dominant wave which decreases on opening the eyes is?
questions.explanation:
The dominant wave, which decreases on opening the eyes, is the Alpha wave. A resting and awake person, when closes his eyes and then opens them to focus attention on something, the alpha rhythm gets replaced by an irregular, low-voltage beta rhythm. This phenomenon is known as alpha block. This can be produced by any form of sensory stimulation or mental concentration, such as solving arithmetic problems. This is also known as the arousal or alerting response because it is correlated with the aroused, alert state. It has also been called desynchronization because it represents the breaking up of the synchronised neural activity necessary to produce regular waves. However, the term desynchronization is misleading because the rapid EEG activity seen in the alert state is also synchronised, but at a higher rate. Pearl PM0901: EEG Waves

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question:
10. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex typically leads to 

1. Hypopnea
2. Bradycardia
3. Hypotension 
4. Tachycardia
questions.explanation:
The Bezold-Jarisch reflex typically leads to hypopnea, bradycardia and hypotension. The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a cardiovascular response triggered by chemosensitive vagal C fibres in the heart and lungs, leading to profound bradycardia, hypotension, and a brief period of apnea, followed by rapid, shallow breathing. It can be activated by substances like capsaicin, serotonin, phenylbiguanide, and veratridine. and serotonin or during myocardial ischemia and coronary angiography, contributing to hypotension in heart disease. It also serves a protective role by limiting toxic substance absorption from the lungs. This reflex can be activated during myocardial ischemia and reperfusion because of increased production of oxygen radicals and by agents used as radiocontrast for coronary angiography. Activation of cardiopulmonary chemosensitive receptors may also be part of a defence mechanism protecting individuals from toxic chemical hazards, and it may help reduce the amount of inspired pollutants that get absorbed into the blood. This protects vital organs from the potential toxicity of these pollutants and facilitates their elimination. Vasovagal syncope has also been attributed to activation of the Bezold–Jarisch reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: 12. The neural center responsible for explicit memory is
questions.explanation:
The hippocampus is the neural centre responsible for explicit memory. Forms of memory are classified into two types, explicit and implicit: * Explicit/declarative memory is the memory of factual knowledge about people, places, things, and events. It is associated with consciousness/awareness. It is of 2 types: * * Semantic memory (facts), e.g., knowing the capital of India, date of birth, names of people, etc. The parts of the brain involved are the lateral and anterior temporal cortex, as well as the prefrontal cortex. * Episodic memory (events), e.g., recalling the events that occurred on the first day in college. The parts of the brain involved are the hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, and neocortex.  * Implicit memory/Non-declarative memory does not involve consciousness or awareness. It is of 4 types: * * Procedural memory refers to skills and habits, which, once acquired, become unconscious and automatic, such as riding a bicycle or driving a car. It is processed in the striatum. * Priming refers to the facilitation of the recognition of words or objects by prior exposure to them. It is dependent on the neocortex. * Non-associative learning includes habituation and sensitisation. It is dependent on various reflex pathways. * Associative learning includes classical and operant conditioning, in which one learns about the relationship between one stimulus and another. It is dependent on the amygdala for its emotional responses and the cerebellum for its motor responses. Pearl PM0907: Forms of Memory From physiologic point of view memory is divided into explicit and implicit forms.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: 13. The murmur of mitral stenosis corresponds to which part of the ECG?
questions.explanation:
The murmur of mitral stenosis corresponds to the P wave of the ECG. Mitral stenosis leads to increased pressure in the left atrium. Left atrial abnormality may cause broad, notched P waves in the limb leads and a biphasic P wave in lead V1 with a prominent negative component representing delayed depolarisation of the left atria. P wave may become tall and peaked in the lead II and upright in lead V1 due to severe pulmonary hypertension or when tricuspid stenosis complicates mitral stenosis, leading to right atrial enlargement. The QRS complex is usually normal. In severe pulmonary hypertension, right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy can be seen.   Auscultatory findings in mitral stenosis are: * A mid-diastolic murmur * The first heart sound (S1) is accentuated * The opening snap (OS) is after the A2 sound. It is best heard during the expiration and at the apex of the heart * The OS is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is heard best at the apex with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position. This murmur correlates with the severity of the stenosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: 14. Which of the following pulses can be best explained by Frank-Starling law?
questions.explanation:
Pulsus Alternans can be explained by the Frank-Starling law.  Frank-Starling law of the heart states relationship between end-diastolic volume and stroke volume is best represented by the length-tension relationship. The volume of blood ejected by the ventricle depends on the volume present in the ventricle at the end of diastole. The length of the myocytes depends on the volume (and hence tension) present at the end of the diastole, which in turn, depends on the volume returned to the heart, or the venous return. It governs normal ventricular function and ensures that cardiac output equals venous return, within physiological limits. Pulsus Alternans is seen in left ventricular dysfunction in heart failure and is characterised by alternating strong and weak pulses due to reduced left ventricular contraction in every other cardiac cycle. When the left ventricular contractility is reduced, there is a decrease in stroke volume, leading to a weak pulse and increased residual volume within the ventricles. This increase in residual volume leads to increased end-diastolic volume in the next cardiac cycle, leading to stronger ventricular contractility, greater stroke volume and a stronger pulse. Hence, pulsus alternans follows the Frank-Starling law of the heart.

Other options: Option A: Pulsus Parvus refers to a weak pulse. Aortic stenosis presents with pulsus parvus et tardus, which is seen as a low-amplitude pulse that rises slowly and has a late peak. Option B: Pulsus Bisferiens is a pulse with double peaks. Option D: Pulsus Paradoxus refers to a fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration. Pearl PM0170: Cardiac parameters

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: 15. The hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient in case of severe diarrhoea is due to
options: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney
Decreased absorption of sodium from the gut
questions.explanation:
The hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient in case of severe diarrhoea is due to increased secretion of Anti-diuretic hormone (ADH).  Anti-diuretic hormone, also known as Vasopressin, gets activated in severe diarrhoea, leading to dilutional hyponatremia due to increased water reabsorption from the kidneys. In severe diarrhoea, there is hyponatremia due to increased loss of sodium through faeces, leading to decreased absorption of sodium from the gut. The body also tries to maintain homeostasis by activating the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to increased secretion of aldosterone, which further leads to an increase in sodium reabsorption from the kidneys. Note: Among options B and C, the best answer is Option C, as it is a more primary mechanism for maintaining homeostasis of water and electrolytes.
